title: Final Project: Employee Management & Payroll System
summary: Capstone portfolio project: build, test, and publish a multi-class OOP application ready for GitHub.

activities.title: Practical Context: Comprehensive Enterprise Payroll Portfolio Capstone

realWorldMetaphor.scenario: On the 28th of every month at a Fortune 500 company, thousands of different workers receive their pay: corporate executives on annual salaried retainers, software consultants billing hourly timesheets, and sales directors earning base retainers plus percentage sales commissions. Nobody manually types checks. A centralized payroll engine iterates across every employee record, invokes their individual compensation algorithm, deducts state and federal taxes according to local tax policies, deposits the net pay into bank accounts, and prints an immutable, tamper-proof paystub for audit records.
realWorldMetaphor.mapping: In software development, this Capstone Payroll System is the ultimate synthesis of all Object-Oriented Programming concepts: 1) Encapsulation & Value Objects (`EmployeeId`, `PaySlip`), 2) Inheritance & Polymorphism (`Employee` base class with `SalariedEmployee`, `HourlyEmployee`, and `CommissionEmployee`), 3) Abstraction (`Payable` interface), 4) Composition (Departments containing Employees, Employees composing Roles/Taxes), and 5) Layered Service Architecture (`PayrollEngine` collaborating with `TaxStrategy` and `AuditNotifier`).
realWorldMetaphor.takeaway: The Capstone synthesizes all OOP principles into a production-grade, portfolio-ready GitHub system.

activities.content:
This capstone build represents the culmination of all Java Object-Oriented Programming concepts.

You will design a complete, production-grade enterprise system featuring:
- Abstract employee base classes with constructor chaining.
- Specialized salaried, hourly, and commissioned employee subclasses.
- Layered repository storage and payroll dispatch.

This project delivers a portfolio-ready demonstration of professional OOP mastery.

activities.title: Capstone: Employee Management & Payroll System Architecture
The Polymorphic Employee Compensation Hierarchy
activities.explanation: Illustrates dynamic polymorphism: SalariedEmployee and HourlyEmployee calculate earnings through customized business formulas under the common Payable contract.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `Payable` provides the top-level contract for anything that generates compensation.
`HourlyEmployee` calculates standard rate plus 1.5x overtime for hours exceeding 40.

activities.title: The Enterprise Payroll Engine and Auditable PaySlips
activities.explanation: Coordinates payroll processing: PayrollEngine applies TaxStrategy across Department staff and generates immutable PaySlip records.

stepByStepWalkthrough.description: `PaySlip` is an immutable record capturing financial state.
`PayrollEngine.processDepartment()` computes gross, tax, and net for each employee.

activities.title: Knowledge Assessment: The Capstone Payroll System

questions.question: Why is `Payable` defined as an interface rather than forcing all paid entities to inherit from `Employee`?
options: Interfaces are always faster to execute than abstract classes
To allow non-employee entities (such as Independent Contractor, Vendor Invoice, or Charity Donation) to be processed by the payroll engine without belonging to the employee hierarchy
Because abstract classes cannot have methods
To prevent garbage collection
questions.explanation: Interfaces provide capability contracts (e.g. Payable) that can be implemented across diverse, unrelated class hierarchies.

questions.question: Why is `PaySlip` modeled as an Immutable Value Object?
options: Because financial records must be audit-proof, tamper-proof, and safe from unexpected modification once issued
Because immutable objects require no heap memory
Java records cannot have getters
To prevent the compiler from optimizing bytecode
questions.explanation: Financial transactions and paystubs are historical records of audit fact that should never be mutated after generation.

questions.question: How does `PayrollEngine` follow the Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)?
options: It creates a new database connection inside its constructor
It depends on abstractions like `TaxStrategy` and `Payable` rather than concrete classes like `CaliforniaTax` or `SalariedEmployee`
It makes all methods static
It prevents inheritance
questions.explanation: DIP states high-level modules should not depend on low-level modules; both should depend on abstractions.

questions.question: How does the Template Method pattern assist in designing the `Employee` base class?
options: It defines common identity state and invariant checks while leaving specific gross pay calculations to concrete subclasses
It forces all methods to be final
It requires using XML templates
It replaces all constructors
questions.explanation: The Template Method allows the base class to define common structure and workflow while deferring specific variant steps to subclasses.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of making `Department` an Aggregate Root?
options: It allows searching employees without an index
It encapsulates the staff list and enforces department-wide invariants (like max team capacity or total department payroll budgets)
It turns all staff into singletons
It enables multiple inheritance
questions.explanation: An Aggregate Root manages access to its children, preventing external callers from modifying staff rosters without invariant validation.

questions.question: If we want to introduce a `CommissionEmployee` (base salary + sales commission), what changes are needed in `PayrollEngine`?
options: PayrollEngine must be rewritten from scratch
Add a new `if/else` statement inside `processDepartment`
Zero changes: because `CommissionEmployee` implements `Payable`, the engine processes it via dynamic polymorphism (Open-Closed Principle)
Recompile the JVM
questions.explanation: Because `PayrollEngine` works with the `Payable` abstraction, new employee types can be added without changing the engine.

questions.question: Why is testing the Capstone system straightforward?
options: Because it uses zero external frameworks, uses constructor injection, and entities have clear inputs and outputs
Because Vitest only tests Java
Because Java does not require test assertions
Because all variables are public
questions.explanation: Clean OOP with constructor injection and pure domain models makes isolated unit testing fast, deterministic, and mock-friendly.

questions.question: What should a professional GitHub README for this Capstone include?
options: Only the author's name
System Overview, Architecture / Class Diagram, Design Patterns Used, Key OOP Concepts Demonstrated, and Instructions to Run Tests
A copy of the Java specification manual
Raw compiler bytecode
questions.explanation: A stellar GitHub portfolio project features a professional overview, UML/architecture diagram, design decisions, and execution instructions.

questions.question: What design pattern is used by having `TaxStrategy` injected into `PayrollEngine`?
options: Strategy Pattern
Flyweight Pattern
Memento Pattern
Interpreter Pattern
questions.explanation: The Strategy pattern defines a family of interchangeable tax computation algorithms encapsulated in independent classes.

questions.question: How does this Capstone prepare you for FAANG low-level design (LLD) interviews?
options: It teaches you how to memorize LeetCode answers
It demonstrates end-to-end translation of ambiguous business rules into solid, testable, modular OOP classes adhering to SOLID principles
It guarantees an offer letter without interviewing
It replaces data structures and algorithms
questions.explanation: The Capstone demonstrates complete end-to-end design fluency: entity modeling, SOLID adherence, polymorphic dispatch, and separation of concerns.

activities.title: FAANG Technical Interview: The Capstone Portfolio Presentation

questions.question: Walk me through how you architected this Employee Management & Payroll System from scratch.
questions.answer: I started by establishing clean domain abstractions: 1) Defined `Payable` as the root capability interface to allow non-employee entities (contractors, vendors) to be paid seamlessly. 2) Built an abstract `Employee` class encapsulating identity, name, and department invariants. 3) Created polymorphic specializations (`SalariedEmployee`, `HourlyEmployee`, `CommissionEmployee`) with domain-specific compensation rules like 1.5x overtime. 4) Decoupled tax calculation via a polymorphic `TaxStrategy` injected into `PayrollEngine`. 5) Emitted immutable `PaySlip` value objects to ensure historical financial auditability. This strictly respects all 5 SOLID principles.
questions.keyTakeaway: Structure the narrative around domain boundaries, polymorphic abstractions, and SOLID principles.
keyPoints: Payable interface decouples payment from employee taxonomy
Polymorphic subclasses encapsulate specific gross pay math
Tax calculations decoupled via Strategy pattern
Immutable PaySlip ensures audit trail integrity

questions.question: How did you ensure that adding a new employee type does not risk breaking existing payroll disbursements?
questions.answer: By honoring the Open-Closed Principle. The `PayrollEngine` iterates across collections of the `Payable` interface. When business adds a new compensation model—say, `PieceworkEmployee` who gets paid per unit assembled—we simply author a new class `PieceworkEmployee implements Payable`. We write unit tests for `calculateGrossPay()`. We never touch or recompile the `PayrollEngine`, `TaxStrategy`, or existing `SalariedEmployee` classes. The blast radius of the new feature is completely contained.
questions.keyTakeaway: Polymorphism against interface abstractions reduces the blast radius of new business features to zero.
keyPoints: PayrollEngine depends only on the Payable interface
New employee classes are purely additive
Zero risk of regression on existing salary calculations

questions.question: Why did you choose to make PaySlip immutable rather than an editable entity?
questions.answer: In financial systems, once a payment is calculated and disbursed, that transaction represents an immutable historical event. If `PaySlip` were mutable with setters, a rogue method or bug in a downstream notification listener could alter the `netPay` or `taxDeduction`, causing accounting discrepancies between the printed payslip and the ledger. By making all fields `private final` and omitting setters, `PaySlip` is inherently thread-safe, safe for caching, and guaranteed to be tamper-proof.
questions.keyTakeaway: Financial audit artifacts must be immutable value objects to prevent state corruption.
keyPoints: Disbursed paystubs are historical facts that must not mutate
Immutability guarantees thread safety across concurrent readers
Prevents downstream side-effects from altering financial records

questions.question: How would you extend this system to support international tax jurisdictions across 20 countries?
questions.answer: I would expand the `TaxStrategy` into a jurisdictional Strategy Factory. We create `JurisdictionTaxStrategy` implementations (e.g. `UsFederalTax`, `UkHmrctax`, `GermanSteuerTax`). An `Employee` would compose their tax jurisdiction identifier or residence country. When `PayrollEngine` processes an employee, it queries `TaxStrategyFactory.getStrategy(employee.getCountryCode())` and computes the appropriate localized tax, social security, and health deductions, maintaining complete decoupling from employee compensation logic.
questions.keyTakeaway: Combine the Strategy and Factory patterns to scale business rules across global dimensions.
keyPoints: Strategy implementations for each national tax authority
Factory maps country code to concrete strategy
PayrollEngine remains agnostic to national tax laws

questions.question: How did you design the Department class to enforce team budget limits?
questions.answer: I treated `Department` as an Aggregate Root. `Department` holds a `private final double budgetCap` and a `private final List<Employee> staff`. When adding a new employee via `department.addEmployee(e)`, the department calculates the projected monthly payroll including the new employee. If the total exceeds `budgetCap`, it rejects the addition and throws a domain `BudgetExceededException`. External callers cannot bypass this rule because the internal staff list is never exposed as a mutable reference.
questions.keyTakeaway: Aggregate Roots guard business budget invariants across internal collections.
keyPoints: Department acts as Aggregate Root managing staff
Invariant validation prevents exceeding allocated budget
Protects internal collections from direct external mutation

questions.question: How do you present this project on your resume and GitHub to stand out to FAANG recruiters?
questions.answer: I highlight architectural impact rather than basic syntax: 'Engineered a modular, multi-tier Employee Management & Payroll System in Java applying SOLID principles, Strategy and Template Method patterns, and immutable domain records. Achieved 100% test coverage with automated unit test suites validating polymorphic overtime formulas, budget constraint invariants, and tax deductions. Published production-grade GitHub repository with comprehensive architectural diagrams and technical documentation.'
questions.keyTakeaway: Emphasize architectural depth, design patterns, testing rigor, and business impact.
keyPoints: Lead with SOLID principles and design patterns applied
Highlight test automation and invariant validation
Document system architecture with clear diagrams

practiceProblems.title: Warmup: Building Commission Employee Extension
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
In the provided starter code, complete `CommissionEmployee` extending `Employee`:
1. Private fields: `baseSalary` (double), `salesAmount` (double), `commissionRate` (double).
2. Constructor initializes super(id, name, department) and fields.
3. Override `calculateGrossPay()`: returns `baseSalary + (salesAmount * commissionRate)`.
In `main()` test with `new CommissionEmployee("E-03", "Sam", "Sales", 2000.0, 50000.0, 0.05)` and print `'Gross: $' + emp.calculateGrossPay()` (should be 4500.0).
hints: Call super(id, name, dept) in the constructor.

practiceProblems.title: Scratch: Modeling the Immutable PaySlip Value Object
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build the immutable PaySlip value object from scratch without starter code:
1. Class `PaySlip`: private final `payeeId` (String), private final `gross` (double), private final `tax` (double), private final `net` (double).
2. Constructor takes `(String payeeId, double gross, double taxRate)`: computes `tax = gross * taxRate` and `net = gross - tax`.
3. Provide getters for all four fields.
4. Method `String getSummary()`: returns `payeeId + ' -> Gross: $' + gross + ', Net: $' + net`.
5. In `Main`:
   - Create `new PaySlip("EMP-55", 4000.0, 0.20)` (20% tax)
   - Print `slip.getSummary()`
   - Print `'Tax deducted: $' + slip.getTax()` (800.0).
hints: All fields are private final with no setters, making PaySlip immutable.

practiceProblems.title: Scratch: Department Budget Invariant Guard
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build a budget-guarded Department aggregate from scratch without starter code:
1. Interface `PayableMember`: `String getName()`, `double getMonthlyCost()`.
2. Class `StaffMember implements PayableMember`: `name` (String), `cost` (double). Getters.
3. Class `DepartmentAggregate`: `name` (String), `maxBudget` (double), private list of `PayableMember`.
   - Method `boolean addStaff(PayableMember m)`: computes current total cost + m.getMonthlyCost(). If total > maxBudget, returns false (rejected!). Otherwise adds to list and returns true.
   - Method `double getTotalExpenditure()`: sums monthly costs of current staff.
4. In `Main`:
   - Create department with budget 10000.0
   - Add staff1 (cost 6000.0) -> returns true
   - Add staff2 (cost 5000.0) -> returns false (would exceed 10000)
   - Print `'Total Expenditure: $' + dept.getTotalExpenditure()` (6000.0).
practiceProblems.expectedOutput:
Added Alice: true
Added Bob: false
Total Expenditure: $6000.0

practiceProblems.title: Bug Hunt: Fixing Overtime Calculation Bug
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
In the provided buggy code, `HourlyContractor.calculateGross()` has an overtime bug: it pays 1.5x on ALL hours worked instead of only on the hours exceeding 40!
Refactor `HourlyContractor`:
1. If `hours <= 40`, pay `hours * rate`.
2. If `hours > 40`, pay `(40 * rate) + ((hours - 40) * rate * 1.5)`.
3. In `main()` test with rate 50.0 and 50 hours (should be 40*50 + 10*75 = 2000 + 750 = 2750.0).

practiceProblems.title: Advanced: Complete Enterprise Payroll Disbursement Simulation
practiceProblems.problemStatement:
Build the complete end-to-end Enterprise Payroll System from scratch without starter code:
1. Interface `PayableRecord`: `String getId()`, `double computeEarnings()`.
2. Strategy Interface `TaxEngine`: `double calculateTax(double earnings)`.
3. Class `FlatTaxEngine implements TaxEngine`: 10% tax (`earnings * 0.10`).
4. Class `SalariedStaff implements PayableRecord`: `id` (String), `salary` (double). `computeEarnings()` returns `salary`.
5. Class `AuditedPayrollProcessor`: constructor receives `TaxEngine`.
   - Method `double disburseTotalNet(List<PayableRecord> records)`: iterates records, calculates earnings, subtracts tax, sums net payouts, and returns total net.
6. In `Main`:
   - Create list of 2 records: `SalariedStaff("S-1", 3000.0)` and `SalariedStaff("S-2", 5000.0)` (Total gross = 8000.0)
   - With 10% tax, total tax = 800.0, total net = 7200.0
   - Run `disburseTotalNet()` and print `'Total Net Disbursed: $' + totalNet`.
